KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...
A weak front will cross Northern New England this afternoon with 
clouds continuing to increase as it does so. Forecast soundings 
remain quite dry in the low levels, which should keep most dry, 
other than maybe a few sprinkles or light showers here and there. 
The exception will be across southern NH and maybe as far north as 
Portland where a wave crossing southern New England will bring in 
more low-level moisture and a slightly better chance for light 
showers and measurable precip this evening. These same areas may see 
a couple of additional light showers overnight, but accumulations 
are likely to remain light and less than a tenth of an inch by 
daybreak Friday. Elsewhere, skies should thin out behind the front 
overnight with temperatures a bit cooler than last night. This puts 
lows mostly in the 50s, but some northern valley could dip into the 
40s. More valley fog is expected, especially along the CT River.

High pressure builds in behind the front for Friday, keeping things 
mostly dry, although an occasional light shower or two can't be 
discounted along the coast or southern NH during the day and again 
Friday night due to be in closer proximity to a weak low/surface 
trough developing south of Long Island. Highs should away from the 
coast should be in the mid 70s to low 80s, except onshore flow and 
more clouds could keep southern NH and coastal spots a bit cooler. 
Lows again are forecast to be mostly in the 50s but could again be 
in the 40s across the north depending on the clouds. 

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...

A front that initially appears stalled will begin moving northward 
as a warm front on Saturday, bringing unsettled weather with 
multiple chances for precipitation as multiple waves of low pressure 
ride along it. A 500 mb trough approaching from the west is 
likely to interact with another wave arriving from the south on 
a low-level southerly flow, likely driving surface low 
development. Models highlight two potential outcomes for this 
interaction: either a full phase of the two waves resulting in a
potential locally heavy rainfall event, or a split setup with 
two distinct rainfall maxima that could shift the heaviest 
totals outside of interior portions of our CWA. While timing 
discrepancies persist between short-range models showing early 
arrival and outliers suggesting a much slower progression, most 
models are anticipating up to three quarters of an inch towards
the coast, with localized totals potentially nearing an inch. 
Temperatures throughout the period are expected to remain right
around seasonal for this time of year with mild overnight lows.

As the trough moves across the Great Lakes, SW flow aids in
moisture advection into the Northeast. Ensemble probabilities
place the greatest IVT just off the New England coast where
around 2 inches of PWAT resides. Values aren't expected to be
this high over land. Low level moisture will be the most ready
to advect into the coast and interior as a disturbance moves
into the Gulf of Maine, but residual mid and upper level dry air
could limit coverage of showers Saturday. So while forecast rain
chances encompass much of the forecast area, the morning and
early afternoon are currently not expected be a washout for
interior and mountain locations. Dry air will ultimately be
fighting a losing battle as the trough moves east. IVT improves,
as does PWAT across the interior overnight into Sunday. As
clouds thicken, upper low from the Great Lakes will have a broad
precip field that moves into NH and western ME Sunday morning.
This should again bring intermittent periods of showers, but
rainfall totals may be limited by escaping PWATs.

KEY MESSAGE 3 DESCRIPTION...

The 500 mb trough develops a closed low and will keep high- 
elevation shower chances going into the start of the week. This
eventually departs northward into the eastern Canadian Shield 
by Wednesday. 

Temperatures and nighttime lows will remain seasonal for this 
time of year as precipitation chances wane through the middle of
the week from the return of high pressure. The next chance for
widespread rainfall returns towards the end of next week.
